    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-1016-j-pragma-2018-03-015",
      "title": "‘But what is the reason why you know such things?’: Question and response patterns in the LADO interview",
      "research_question": "What recurrent question-response and repair patterns create interactional problems in LADO interviews, and how might those problems be avoided or resolved?",
      "methodology": "The authors applied Conversation Analysis to five recorded face-to-face LADO interviews with female African asylum seekers selected from a set of twelve interviews recorded between 2008 and 2011. They transcribed the interactions using a subset of standard CA conventions and classified recurrent question and response patterns, combining detailed sequential qualitative analysis with limited frequency counts. The five interviews contained 602 classified question tokens across 133 minutes and 22 seconds of interaction. The analysis focused especially on directives, multiple questions, echo questions, challenges, and repair.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "When an interviewer bundled a broad directive with more specific questions, interviewees generally answered the most specific and/or most recent question rather than carrying out the broader directive.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§4.1.1 Directives in multiple questions; §5 Conclusion and recommendations"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Sequential analysis shows that an apparently unanswered broad question can result from the interviewer immediately narrowing it to a yes/no or otherwise specific question, leaving no interactional opportunity to answer the original request.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§4.1.1 Directives in multiple questions"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Directives intended to elicit language samples worked more effectively when the interviewer supplied a concrete topic for extended talk rather than issuing an underspecified request to speak.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§4.1.2 Directives to elicit language samples; §5 Conclusion and recommendations"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Echo questions were predominantly treated as confirmation requests and could therefore fail when interviewers intended them as prompts for elaboration or repair initiators.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§4.1.3 Echo questions"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Questions framed as challenges, including negative questions, source-of-knowledge challenges, turn-initial but, and hostile reformulations, contributed to confrontational interaction while producing little apparent information-gathering benefit.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§4.2 Challenges; §5 Conclusion and recommendations"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Some question sequences ended without a satisfactory answer and were abandoned after unsuccessful repair attempts, showing that nonresponse can persist at the level of a line of questioning rather than a single adjacent turn.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§4.3 Repair; §5 Conclusion and recommendations"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Across the five interviews, positive wh-questions were the most frequent question type, followed by positive yes/no questions, with 602 total classified question tokens.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§4 and Table 2"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "Only five interviews were analyzed, so the authors explicitly caution against overgeneralization.",
        "All analyzed interviews came from a single source and all interviewees were female.",
        "Inter-interviewer differences were not examined even though some interviewers appeared in multiple recordings.",
        "Prosody was not incorporated into the analysis because participants were largely non-native English speakers and suitable comparative prosodic research was unavailable.",
        "The authors could not account systematically for sequential conversational norms from the interviewees' relevant African languages and cultures.",
        "The study is an institutional interview study rather than workplace email, so its evidence about multi-question response scope does not directly establish email behavior."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": false,

      },

      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "The study analyzes question-response structures in five LADO interviews with female asylum seekers.",
        "Directives are frequently combined with additional questions in a single interviewer turn.",
        "Recipients tend to respond first to the most specific or most recent component of a multiple question.",
        "A broad directive can appear unanswered because the interviewer immediately supplies a narrower question.",
        "Specific topic guidance makes requests for language samples easier for interviewees to fulfill.",
        "Echo questions are most commonly treated as requests for confirmation.",
        "An echo intended to solicit elaboration may instead receive only confirmation.",
        "Challenges contribute to a hostile or confrontational interactional environment.",
        "Repair can resolve simple misunderstandings but can become disruptive when mutual understanding is not quickly achieved.",
        "Some lines of questioning are eventually abandoned without a satisfactory answer.",
        "The five recordings contain 602 classified question tokens over 133 minutes and 22 seconds."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/129996/1/Problems_in_the_LADO_Interview_final_with_full_refs.pdf",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-3115-1708376-1708429",
      "title": "Contrasting the Interaction Structure of an Email and a Telephone Corpus: A Machine Learning Approach to Annotation of Dialogue Function Units",
      "research_question": "Can a common Dialogue Function Unit annotation scheme represent initiation-response structure in workplace email and telephone dialogue, and how accurately can dialogue acts and response links be predicted in the two modalities?",
      "methodology": "The authors annotated Dialogue Function Units, dialogue acts, and forward/backward response links in 48 Loqui telephone dialogues and 122 Enron email threads. Their scheme represents requests with forward links, responses with backward links, unanswered requests as dangling forward links, and responses to non-request antecedents through secondary forward links. They compared the distributions of acts and links across the two corpora and evaluated heuristic, regular SVM, and structured SVM models for dialogue-act tagging and response-link prediction. Experiments used five-fold cross-validation while assuming gold DFU segmentation.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "The annotation scheme permits response relations that are non-adjacent and that originate either from explicit requests or from preceding non-request discourse units, making it more general than a strict adjacent question-answer model.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§3 Annotation Scheme"
        },
        {
          "finding": "An explicit request with no matching response is represented as a dangling forward link, providing a direct annotation mechanism for unanswered questions or requests.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§3 Annotation Scheme"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Dangling links were proportionally more common in Enron email than in Loqui telephone dialogue, at 7% versus 2% in the reported link statistics.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§4 Corpora; Table 2"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Only 28% of Enron DFUs participated as first or second parts of links, compared with 63% in Loqui, and Enron links more often involved secondary forward links than overt request-response pairs.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§4 Corpora; Table 2"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Dialogue-act tagging was substantially easier than response-link prediction: structured-SVM dialogue-act accuracy was 88.71% on Enron and 70.26% on Loqui, while paired-link F1 was 34.88% and 49.38% respectively.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§6 Experiments; Tables 4 and 5"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Email was easier than Loqui for dialogue-act classification but harder for link prediction, so the hypothesis that Enron would simply be the harder corpus was only task-dependent.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§6 Experiments and §7 Discussion"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The manual data contain a small number of multiple backward links, but the prediction systems impose at most one forward link of each type and one backward link per DFU and the structured model additionally forbids crossing links.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§4 Table 2; §5.3 Regular SVM; §5.4 Structured SVM"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "DFU segmentation is assumed to be given rather than predicted automatically.",
        "Most of each corpus was annotated by a single annotator after the initial guideline-development stage, limiting direct reliability evidence for the complete annotated collections.",
        "The link predictors restrict each DFU to at most one link of each modeled type even though the complete manual annotation is not constrained in that way.",
        "The structured model prohibits crossing links, while the gold annotations are evaluated without that restriction.",
        "The Enron and Loqui corpora differ simultaneously in modality, domain, participant structure, and communicative goals, so observed differences cannot be attributed purely to email versus telephone modality.",
        "The Enron link set is relatively small, particularly for some response-link subtypes.",
        "The paper does not separately model proposition-level partial answers to several propositions bundled inside one DFU."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": false,
        "dataset_available": false,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "nonadjacent_response_links": 0.99,
        "dangling_links_encode_unanswered_requests": 0.99,
        "more_dangling_links_in_email": 0.99,
        "email_has_fewer_linked_dfus": 0.99,
        "link_prediction_harder_than_da_tagging": 0.99,
        "email_difficulty_is_task_dependent": 0.98,
        "model_restricts_multi_links": 0.99
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "A Dialogue Function Unit is annotated with a dialogue act and can participate in forward or backward response links.",
        "Requests for information and action receive forward links.",
        "A response receives a backward link to the discourse unit it answers or otherwise responds to.",
        "A request that receives no matching response is represented by a dangling forward link.",
        "Responses can also link to earlier assertions that did not originally carry a request link.",
        "The study annotates 48 Loqui telephone dialogues and 122 Enron email threads.",
        "Enron contains a higher proportion of dangling links than Loqui.",
        "Link prediction performs markedly worse than dialogue-act prediction.",
        "Response links in email are often structurally distant from the discourse units to which they respond.",
        "The manual annotation contains a few DFUs with multiple backward links.",
        "The prediction algorithms constrain the number and configuration of links more strongly than the manual annotation."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://aclanthology.org/W09-3953.pdf",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-5210-dad-2022-203",
      "title": "Characterizing the Response Space of Questions: data and theory",
      "research_question": "Can a broad empirically grounded taxonomy and formal theory characterize the range of responses that natural-language questions receive across different dialogue genres and languages?",
      "methodology": "The authors developed a taxonomy of question responses and applied it to 2,934 question-response pairs from the English BNC, BEE, MapTask, and Cornell Movie corpora and the Polish Spokes corpus. Question-response pairs were annotated with categories including direct and indirect answers, clarification responses, acknowledgments, dependent questions, several kinds of evasive response, and an OTHER category; BNC and Spokes subsets received multi-annotator reliability analysis. They compared response distributions across corpora and languages and analyzed disagreement patterns. The empirical taxonomy is then given a formal semantic treatment using a dialogue framework.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "The proposed response taxonomy achieved greater than 99.5% coverage in each of the four English corpora because fewer than 0.5% of responses required the OTHER category.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§6.1 English"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Direct answers were the largest response category in every corpus, ranging from 54.67% to 88.93% across the English corpora and accounting for 64.27% of Polish Spokes responses.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§6 Results; Figure 2"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Task-oriented BEE and MapTask dialogues had higher direct-answer rates than free-conversation BNC and Spokes data, indicating substantial genre dependence in response behavior.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§6.3 Discussion"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The direct-answer category theoretically allows partial polar answers and partial wh-answers, but these subcategories were not distinguished in the empirical annotation.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§3 Taxonomy footnote; §8 Formal Analysis"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Annotation disagreements reveal that partiality can affect response classification: the authors note that some partial responses may have been labeled difficult-to-provide-answer because partial answers were not explicitly highlighted in the guidelines.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§7 Annotation reliability and disagreement analysis"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Full-taxonomy agreement on English BNC was moderate to substantial, with Cohen's kappa of 0.7053 and 0.6430 for the two annotator pairings, while a core subset of categories such as direct answers and clarification responses produced near-perfect agreement.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§7.1 Inter-annotator study; Table 6"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Indirect answers were a major source of annotation difficulty and sharply reduced agreement when added to otherwise more reliably distinguished response categories.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§7.1 Inter-annotator study; Table 6"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "Partial polar and partial wh-answers are acknowledged theoretically but were not separately tagged, preventing an empirical estimate of partial-answer frequency or scope.",
        "BEE, MapTask, and CornellMovie were annotated only once, so inter-annotator reliability was directly assessed only for BNC and Spokes.",
        "The English empirical study was restricted to two-person dialogue, excluding multiparty interactions that are common in workplace communication.",
        "The Polish data were not restricted to two-person dialogue because Spokes was the only Polish source, making the English and Polish sampling conditions non-identical.",
        "CornellMovie consists of scripted fictional conversations rather than naturally occurring dialogue.",
        "The study classifies responses to selected questions but does not annotate explicit antecedent graphs for responses that simultaneously address several earlier questions or propositions.",
        "The annotation was not designed to measure whether separate subquestions in a multi-question antecedent were individually answered or left unanswered."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": false,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "taxonomy_coverage": 0.99,
        "direct_answers_dominate": 0.99,
        "genre_affects_response_distribution": 0.98,
        "partial_answers_not_separately_annotated": 0.99,
        "partiality_caused_annotation_difficulty": 0.96,
        "full_taxonomy_reliability": 0.99,
        "indirect_answers_reduce_agreement": 0.99
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "The empirical study contains 2,934 question-response pairs from five corpora.",
        "The taxonomy distinguishes question-specific responses, metacommunicative responses, evasive responses, and residual cases.",
        "Direct answers are the most frequent response type in every corpus examined.",
        "Fewer than half a percent of English responses fall into the residual OTHER class.",
        "Task-oriented dialogues contain proportionally more direct answers than the free-conversation samples.",
        "Partial answers are recognized as possible subtypes of direct answers.",
        "Partial direct answers were not encoded as separate labels during the corpus annotation.",
        "The authors identify partial-answer treatment as a possible source of annotator disagreement in Polish data.",
        "Indirect answers are substantially more difficult to annotate reliably than several core response classes.",
        "The supplementary annotated question-response data and disagreement cases are made available through OSF."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://aclanthology.org/2022.dnd-13.1.pdf",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-18653-v1-2023-findings-acl-710",
      "title": "Discourse Analysis via Questions and Answers: Parsing Dependency Structures of Questions Under Discussion",
      "research_question": "Can document-level discourse structure be parsed as dependency links labeled by free-form Questions Under Discussion, using crowdsourced question-answer annotations instead of a fixed discourse-relation taxonomy?",
      "methodology": "The authors train a two-stage QUD parser on DCQA, a crowdsourced dataset containing more than 22,000 questions across 606 news articles in which each answer sentence is associated with a prior anchor sentence and a question. A Longformer model predicts one prior anchor for each answer sentence, and a GPT-2 question generator produces the QUD, followed by BERT reranking and named-entity masking intended to reduce questions that improperly reveal answer information. They evaluate 380 generated questions from 20 test articles with three human judges, compare QUD structures with RST structures, and conduct a smaller document-simplification case study. The authors release their QUD parsing models.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "The parser represents each non-root sentence as answering a generated question anchored in exactly one earlier sentence, thereby providing explicit response-to-antecedent dependency links over long document context.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§4 Deriving QUD dependency structures"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Human judges rated 71.5% of full-system generated questions as fully plausible at the predicted anchor, and among the high-quality-question subset they rated the targeted sentence as a clear answer 78.8% of the time.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§5.2 Results; Tables 1 and 2"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The answer-scope evaluation distinguishes a clear at-issue answer from a response whose answer content is not the sentence's main point and from a borderline response that is relevant but may not actually address the question.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§5.1 Human Evaluation Setup"
        },
        {
          "finding": "For the full model's evaluated high-quality questions, 3.1% of judgments were in the not-main-point category and 10.5% were in the sort-of category, demonstrating measurable ambiguity in whether a sentence fully addresses a QUD.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§5.2 Results; Table 2"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Reranking and named-entity masking improved question quality; removing reranking reduced fully acceptable Q1 judgments, and removing entity masking produced a much larger decline.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§5.2 Q1 results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "QUD questions were generally more fine-grained than RST relation labels, and showing the QUD increased RST-relation inter-annotator agreement from Krippendorff's alpha 0.158 to 0.216 in the authors' small comparison study.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§3 Questions vs. coherence relations"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The model does not represent relationships among simultaneous or hierarchical questions and does not explicitly model multi-sentence answers, leaving important multi-question and extended-response scope phenomena outside its representation.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§8 Limitations"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "Question relationships and QUD stacks are not modeled, so the representation cannot directly track which subquestions of a larger question remain open.",
        "Each non-root sentence receives one predicted anchor, which excludes multi-antecedent response structures in the parser formulation.",
        "DCQA's setup does not explicitly model multi-sentence answers.",
        "Open-ended QUDs are inherently subjective and the authors state that there is no single uniquely correct QUD structure.",
        "Evaluation relies heavily on human judgments because a satisfactory automatic metric for generated QUD structures is unavailable.",
        "The main training and evaluation domain is news text rather than workplace email or interactive workplace dialogue.",
        "The human evaluation covers 380 questions from 20 DCQA test articles, so it samples only part of the test domain."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": true,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "single_anchor_qud_dependencies": 0.99,
        "human_question_quality": 0.99,
        "graded_answer_scope": 0.99,
        "borderline_answer_rates": 0.99,
        "reranking_and_ner_help": 0.99,
        "qud_more_fine_grained_than_rst": 0.97,
        "question_stacks_and_multisentence_answers_unmodeled": 0.99
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "DCQA contains more than 22,000 crowdsourced questions across 606 news articles.",
        "For every non-root sentence, the parser predicts a prior sentence as its anchor.",
        "A generated natural-language question labels the dependency between the anchor and answer sentence.",
        "The full parser uses Longformer anchor prediction, GPT-2 question generation, BERT reranking, and named-entity masking.",
        "Human evaluation separately asks whether a question is plausible in context and whether the targeted sentence answers it.",
        "The answer judgment distinguishes clear answers from non-main-point answers and borderline relevant responses.",
        "The best system receives a 71.5% fully acceptable rating on question plausibility.",
        "Among questions passing the quality filter, 78.8% of answer judgments are clear yes judgments.",
        "QUD information can align some otherwise divergent RST-relation judgments.",
        "The parser does not model relations among questions or question stacks.",
        "The parser does not explicitly model answers spanning multiple sentences.",
        "The authors release their QUD parsing models."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2210.05905",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-3115-1220355-1220483",
      "title": "Detection of Question-Answer Pairs in Email Conversations",
      "research_question": "Can questions and their corresponding answer segments be detected automatically in asynchronous email threads, and do email-thread structural features improve pairing beyond lexical similarity alone?",
      "methodology": "The authors use an approximately 300-thread corpus containing about 1,000 messages exchanged by the Columbia University ACM student-organization board, with two annotators marking and linking questions and answers. Interrogative question detection is trained with Ripper on 5,000 positive and 5,000 negative Switchboard examples and tested on manually selected ACM email examples. For answer pairing, email messages are segmented by paragraph, each question segment is paired with candidate answer segments from subsequent messages, and lexical, thread-structural, candidate-position, and ancestry features are supplied to a Ripper classifier. Answer-pair experiments use four annotation-derived datasets and five-fold cross-validation.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "About 20% of the email threads in the corpus primarily involved question-answer exchanges, including both one-question/multiple-response and multiple-question/multiple-response configurations.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§1 Introduction"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Email reply structure is not a reliable proxy for response scope because a message sent using Reply or Reply-All can semantically answer an issue raised several messages earlier, and multiple topics can proceed in parallel.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§4 Automatic Answer Detection"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The annotation explicitly permits questions with no corresponding answer, so unanswered questions remain present rather than being removed from the annotated question set.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§4.3 Training Data"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Question-segment identification and question-to-answer linking showed kappa values of 0.68 and 0.81 respectively between the two annotators.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§4.1 Corpus"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The modified interrogative-question detector achieved precision 0.96, recall 0.72, and F1 0.82 after adding handling for questions preceded by declarative material.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§3 Automatic Question Detection; Table 1"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Thread-structural and candidate-position features substantially improved answer-link detection over cosine similarity alone; on the Union data, F1 increased from 0.503 for the lexical baseline to 0.656 with the full feature set.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§4.4 Experiments and Results; Tables 3 and 4"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Separating questions with at most two candidate answer segments from harder cases produced a combined F1 of 0.730, compared with 0.656 on the unsplit Union dataset.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§4.4 Experiments and Results; Table 5"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The system treats paragraphs as discourse segments on the assumption that writers tend to use separate paragraphs for separate issues, so the learned links operate above individual propositions or sentences.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "§4 Automatic Answer Detection"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The email corpus comes from a single university student-organization board and mainly concerns event planning, limiting domain generalizability.",
        "The answer model uses paragraphs as discourse segments, which can collapse several questions or propositions occurring within one paragraph and therefore does not resolve proposition-level partial reply scope.",
        "Candidate answers are drawn from original-content segments in subsequent messages, so the formulation does not cover all possible self-answer or same-message response configurations.",
        "Quoted material was not used as an answer-pairing feature because it was rare in this corpus, even though quotation can explicitly indicate response scope in many workplace email settings.",
        "Automatic question detection was developed for interrogative questions; automatic handling of declarative requests and rhetorical questions remained future work.",
        "The model evaluates binary question-segment/answer-segment links rather than which individual subquestions or propositions inside a multi-question segment are answered.",
        "The paper does not report a public release of the annotated ACM email corpus or experiment code."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": false,
        "dataset_available": false,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "qa_threads_common": 0.98,
        "reply_structure_differs_from_response_scope": 0.99,
        "unanswered_questions_retained": 0.98,
        "annotation_agreement": 0.99,
        "question_detection_performance": 0.99,
        "structural_features_improve_pairing": 0.99,
        "candidate_split_improves_f1": 0.99,
        "paragraph_level_scope": 0.99
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "The ACM corpus contains roughly 300 threads and about 1,000 individual email messages.",
        "Roughly one fifth of the observed threads primarily center on question-answer exchanges.",
        "Several questions and several responses can be pursued in parallel in one email thread.",
        "A semantic response can target an older message rather than the message that is its immediate structural parent.",
        "Some annotated questions have no answer anywhere in the thread.",
        "The authors use paragraphs as discourse segments for answer-link detection.",
        "The annotators achieved higher agreement for question-answer linking than for deciding which segments contain questions.",
        "Lexical similarity by itself is insufficient for reliable question-answer pairing.",
        "Features based on message ancestry, distance, candidate ordering, and thread structure improve answer-link classification.",
        "The modified interrogative-question detector reaches an F1 score of 0.82.",
        "The full Union answer-pairing experiment reaches F1 0.656, and the split-data strategy reaches F1 0.730.",
        "Declarative-form and rhetorical-question detection remained unresolved in the reported system."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://aclanthology.org/C04-1128.pdf",
      "access": "full_text"
    }
  ],
  "skipped": []
}
